A reproducible technical note

Data compression and AI: two names for one thing

Why learning is compression — from Shannon and MDL through PCA, neural codecs and generative models — with weak-lensing examples and a worked demo.
Dr. Dipak Munshi  ·  Advanced Research Fellow, Imperial College London  ·  part of the ML & Stat Notes series  ·  every figure generated by the code described here
information theorycompression MDLPCA / MOPED autoencodersweak lensing inference

Abstract

This note is about one idea: compressing data and learning from it are the same thing. A model that predicts data well can describe it in few bits, and few bits are only possible once you have found real structure — so "fit a model", "find a summary" and "compress" are three names for one activity. We build the idea up in plain steps, from Shannon and Occam's razor through PCA, the cosmologist's MOPED, autoencoders, variational autoencoders and normalizing flows, and keep one foot in weak-lensing cosmology the whole way, because turning a survey's billions of galaxies into a handful of numbers without losing the physics is exactly a compression problem. A worked demo and small pen-and-paper examples (in 1D and 2D) make each idea concrete. The recurring lesson: a good compressor is a good model, and the art of scientific compression is keeping the information that matters — the Fisher information, the non-Gaussian structure — while throwing the rest away.

There is a deep idea that keeps being rediscovered in statistics, information theory and machine learning: compressing data and learning from it are the same activity. To compress a dataset you must find its regularities; to learn from a dataset you must find its regularities. A model that predicts the data well lets you describe it in fewer bits, and a short description is only possible if you have found real structure. This note follows that single thread from Shannon to modern neural networks, and keeps one foot in cosmology throughout — because the central problem of a survey like Euclid or LSST is exactly a compression problem: turn billions of galaxy measurements into a handful of numbers without losing the information that constrains the physics.

1Learning is compression

A good model is a short description. That one sentence connects everything below.

Three classical results make the link precise:

Shannon
the shortest possible average code length for data drawn from a distribution is its entropy bits. The ideal code spends bits on outcome — rare events cost more, likely ones cost less. To reach the floor you need a code built from itself, so the best compressor is the best probabilistic model [1].
MDL
the Minimum Description Length principle: choose the model that minimises — (bits to describe the model) + (bits to describe the data given the model). This is Occam's razor made quantitative: a more complex model only earns its extra description cost if it saves more than that on [2].
Bayes
MDL is essentially Bayesian: is a code length, and the model prior is the cost of describing the model. Choosing the model that compresses best is choosing the model with the highest evidence — the thread that connects this note to my Bayesian toolkit note.

Why this matters for a physicist

If learning is compression, then every fitting problem is secretly asking "what is the shortest honest description of this data?" In cosmology that reframes the whole pipeline: a summary statistic (a power spectrum, a set of peak counts) is a lossy compression of the raw field, and the art is to throw away the bits you do not need while keeping every bit that constrains . The rest of this note is about how to do that well — and how to tell when it has gone wrong.

2Classical compression, in one page

Two families: lossless (keep every bit) and lossy (keep the bits that matter).

Lossless compression rebuilds the data exactly. The key tools are entropy coders — Huffman and, optimally, arithmetic coding — which spend bits per symbol, reaching Shannon's entropy limit when driven by a good predictive model. (This is the hook modern AI exploits in §9.) Dictionary methods such as LZ77/LZ78 (behind ZIP, PNG) instead compress by referring back to repeated substrings.

Worked example (1D): entropy and an optimal code

Take a source emitting four symbols with probabilities . Its entropy is

Assigning each symbol a code of length gives lengths — e.g. 0, 10, 110, 111 (a Huffman code). The average length is bits, exactly : this code is optimal. A naive fixed 2-bit-per-symbol code would use bits — so knowing the distribution buys a 12.5% saving. The better your model of , the shorter the code: that single fact is the whole of lossless compression.

Lossy compression keeps only an approximation, trading fidelity for size — and nearly always works by transform coding: move the data into a basis where it is sparse (a few large coefficients, many near-zero), then keep and quantise only the large ones. JPEG uses the discrete cosine transform; JPEG 2000 uses wavelets. The reason this works is that natural images — and cosmological fields — are smooth with occasional sharp features, which is exactly what a wavelet basis represents compactly.

Weak-lensing connection

Wavelet transform coding is not an analogy here — it is a real mass-mapping tool. The MRLens and GLIMPSE methods represent a weak-lensing convergence map in a wavelet basis and keep only the significant coefficients, which both denoises and compresses the map. The wavelet method in my U-Net note is the same idea; here we use it as a compressor and measure what it keeps.

3Linear compression = PCA / Karhunen–Loève

The optimal linear compressor — and the gateway to compressing cosmology data.

If we restrict ourselves to linear compression — represent each datum by its projection onto fixed directions — there is a provably optimal choice: the top eigenvectors of the data covariance. This is Principal Component Analysis, known in signal processing as the Karhunen–Loève (KL) transform. The eigenvectors are the directions of greatest variance; keeping the largest-variance minimises the mean-squared reconstruction error among all linear codes of size .

where the solve the covariance eigenproblem (largest first) and the code is the numbers . The beauty of KL is that the error it leaves behind is known exactly — it is the variance in the directions you dropped:

So a rapidly falling eigenvalue spectrum means the data is nearly low-dimensional and compresses well. For a stationary field the KL modes are just Fourier modes, so PCA on such a field is compression in Fourier space — which is why it is so natural in cosmology.

But note the word linear: PCA can only rotate and project, so it can only capture second-order (Gaussian) structure. A dataset that lives on a curved low-dimensional surface defeats it — which is exactly where neural compression comes in (§5), and the reason PCA destroys the non-Gaussian information in the demo.

4Compressing cosmology: MOPED

Compress a huge data vector to one number per parameter — without losing the physics.

Cosmology hit the data-compression wall early: likelihood analyses need to invert large covariance matrices, which is impossible for data vectors of millions of elements. The breakthrough was MOPED (Massive Optimal Data compression; Heavens, Jimenez & Lahav 2000 [5]). The idea is beautiful: instead of compressing for fidelity, compress for information. MOPED projects the data onto directions built from the derivative of the model with respect to each parameter, weighted by the noise — giving one compressed number per parameter while provably preserving the Fisher information (the likelihood curvature) near the best fit.

Concretely, for data with covariance and a model mean , the information about a parameter is the Fisher information

MOPED compresses the whole vector to one number per parameter by projecting onto the weighting vectors built from the model gradient:

The one number carries all the Fisher information the full vector had about (for a single parameter, exactly; for many, after orthogonalising).

Worked example (1D): one number, all the information

Suppose we measure noisy copies of a signal whose amplitude we want: , with known template and i.i.d. noise of variance (so , ). MOPED's single compressed number is the matched filter

Its Fisher information about is — identical to the Fisher information of the full -element dataset. We compressed numbers to one and lost nothing about . That is MOPED in miniature, and it is exactly the matched filter a physicist already trusts.

The key shift: compress for Fisher information, not pixels

A million-element shear data vector carries information about maybe six cosmological parameters. MOPED keeps six numbers and throws away the rest — a compression ratio of — with no loss of parameter information if the likelihood is Gaussian. This is the opposite philosophy to JPEG: we do not care whether the map looks right, only whether the parameters are still constrained. Its modern descendant, score compression [6], generalises this and underpins the compressed summaries used in simulation-based inference (§8).

This idea — Karhunen–Loève and MOPED-style compression of cosmological data vectors — is squarely the kind of statistics my own work lives in, and it is the right lens for reading the demo that follows: fidelity and information are not the same thing.

5Neural compression

Autoencoders are nonlinear PCA; modern codecs learn the whole transform.

An autoencoder is a neural network trained to copy its input to its output through a narrow bottleneck. An encoder squeezes the data into a -dimensional code ; a decoder rebuilds it, by minimising the reconstruction loss

Here is the key fact: if and are linear, the optimum of this objective is exactly PCA — the code spans the top- eigenvectors. Add nonlinearities and the encoder can bend and fold the data onto a curved low-dimensional surface no linear projection can reach. An autoencoder is therefore best read as nonlinear PCA.

The full family:

Autoencoder
deterministic code; learned nonlinear compression. The encoder–decoder shape is exactly the one from my U-Net note — a U-Net is an autoencoder with skip connections.
VAE
a variational autoencoder puts a probability distribution in the bottleneck and maximises the evidence lower bound . The two terms are literally distortion and rate — so a VAE is a learned, probabilistic rate–distortion compressor you can also sample from [9].
Learned codecs
end-to-end neural image/video compression (Ballé et al. [8]) jointly learns the transform and the entropy model, optimising the true rate–distortion trade-off directly. These now rival or beat JPEG 2000.

6Demo: compressing weak-lensing maps

PCA vs wavelet vs autoencoder on simulated convergence maps — and the lesson that fidelity ≠ information.

To make this concrete I simulated non-Gaussian weak-lensing convergence maps (64² pixels = 4096 numbers, using the same log-normal field as my U-Net note) and compressed each one three ways, across a range of code sizes:

PCA / KL
the optimal linear compressor (§3): keep the top- principal components.
Wavelet
the sparse classical compressor (§2): keep the largest wavelet coefficients.
Autoencoder
a small learned nonlinear compressor (§5): a convolutional autoencoder with a -number bottleneck, trained from scratch here.

For each I measured two very different things: the reconstruction error (pixel RMSE — fidelity) and how much of the field's non-Gaussian information survived, using the skewness of the one-point distribution as a simple proxy (the real convergence field has skewness driven by its bright peaks; a compressor that flattens the field destroys exactly the signal that distinguishes cosmologies).

The lesson — and why it is a cosmology lesson

At 64× compression the three methods have almost the same RMSE (PCA 0.91, wavelet 0.83, autoencoder 0.88) — yet their recovered skewness is wildly different (PCA 0.7, wavelet 7.2, autoencoder 6.2, against a true value of 4.28). A linear compressor can look perfectly respectable on reconstruction error while silently destroying the non-Gaussian information that carries the cosmological signal, because a linear projection cannot represent the higher-order structure at all.

This is exactly why MOPED compresses for Fisher information rather than fidelity (§4), and exactly why my own higher-order statistics — the bispectrum, skew-spectrum, convergence-map morphology and phase statistics — exist: they are physically chosen compressions that keep the non-Gaussian bits a generic compressor would throw away. The right question is never "how small can I make it?" but "how small can I make it while keeping the information I came for?"

7The information view

Rate–distortion, the information bottleneck, and two kinds of "information".

Rate–distortion theory (Shannon) makes the fidelity–size trade-off precise: for a tolerable distortion , there is a minimum rate — bits per sample — below which you cannot go. Every curve in the demo above is an empirical rate–distortion curve.

Worked example (1D): the rate–distortion of a Gaussian source

For a single Gaussian variable of variance , compressed to squared-error distortion , the rate–distortion function is exactly

Read it off: to halve the distortion () costs exactly extra bits; and once you allow you need zero bits — just output the mean. This is the theoretical floor the autoencoders and codecs of §5 are trying to approach for real, high-dimensional data.

The Information Bottleneck (Tishby, Pereira & Bialek [7]) reframes learning itself in these terms. With the mutual information measuring how many bits carries about , it seeks a representation of the input that is as compressed as possible while keeping the information about a target :

The first term is the rate (compress the input); the second rewards keeping task-relevant information; sets the trade-off. A deep network, on this view, is a stack of ever-more-compressed representations that discard input detail irrelevant to the task — the same "keep the bits that matter" principle as MOPED, in the language of mutual information.

Shannon information vs Fisher information

Two notions of "information" run through this note and are worth separating. Shannon information (entropy, mutual information) measures bits — how many are needed to describe the data. Fisher information measures how sharply the data pin down a parameter. JPEG cares about Shannon; cosmology cares about Fisher. A compression that is excellent by one criterion can be useless by the other — which is the whole point of the demo.

8Compression for inference

Modern parameter estimation is compression followed by inference on the code.

The compression view makes sense of how Stage-IV inference actually works. The field is too big to put in a likelihood, so we compress it to a summary — and then infer parameters from the summary. The summary can be hand-built (power spectrum, peak counts, MOPED coefficients) or learned (a CNN / U-Net that outputs a few numbers). Either way it is a lossy compression chosen to preserve parameter information, and simulation-based inference then turns that code into a posterior without an explicit likelihood.

My higher-order statistics are compression

Seen this way, a summary statistic is a compressor, and the whole game is choosing one that keeps the cosmological information. That reframes my own research: the weak-lensing bispectrum, skew-spectrum, convergence-map morphology and phase statistics are all compressions of the full non-Gaussian field into a few informative numbers — the physically-motivated counterpart to a learned summary, and exactly the information a linear compressor (as the demo showed) would discard.

9Generative models are compressors

The most striking modern statement of "learning = compression".

Because an entropy coder driven by a model reaches a code length of bits, any good generative model is automatically a compressor. This is the sharpest form of "learning = compression", and it is worth making exact.

The exact statement: training loss is compression rate

If the data truly comes from but you code with a model , your expected code length is the cross-entropy, which splits cleanly:

The first term is the entropy — the hard floor no model can beat. The second is the compression gap: the price, in bits, of an imperfect model, and it is exactly the quantity a network minimises when it is trained by maximum likelihood (log-loss). So the test log-loss of a model, measured in bits per symbol, is its compression rate — "bits per token" and "bits per pixel" are compression ratios, not just loss values.

This is not a metaphor. In 2023, DeepMind drove an arithmetic coder with a large language model and showed that LLMs are state-of-the-art lossless compressors — a model trained only to predict the next token compressed ImageNet image patches to about 43% of their raw size (beating PNG's ~58%) and speech to about 17% (beating FLAC's ~30%), despite never being designed for either [10]. The better the model predicts, the fewer bits it needs; prediction quality and compression ratio are literally the same number.

The generative models in my other notes are compressors for the same reason, and some give an exact code length:

Normalizing flows
an invertible map gives the density exactly by change of variables, , so is a directly usable code length.
VAEs & diffusion
their variational bound (the negative ELBO of §5) is an upper bound on the code length, and "bits-back" coding achieves it — latent-variable models are practical lossless compressors.
Kolmogorov
at the horizon sits the ideal , the length of the shortest program that outputs the data — the ultimate, uncomputable compressor (Solomonoff's induction). Every method here is a computable approximation to it.

Weak lensing: generative models as compressed simulations

This is already how cosmology uses deep generative models. A GAN, flow or diffusion emulator trained on an expensive suite of weak-lensing simulations is a compression of the whole suite into the network weights: megabytes of parameters stand in for terabytes of -body runs, and new maps are decompressed on demand in milliseconds. And a flow-based field-level likelihood plays both roles at once — it is a generative model of convergence maps and the code against which a map is compressed, so its quality is measured in exactly the bits-per-map sense above. The better the model captures the non-Gaussian structure of the field, the shorter the code and the more information it preserves — which brings us to the deepest link in this note.

The key relation: code length, the score, and the Fisher matrix

Write the code length for data under a model with parameters as (nats). Two derivatives connect everything:

Read in words: the score is how much the code length changes when you nudge a parameter, and the Fisher matrix is the curvature of the expected code length around the truth — how sharply the number of bits responds to the cosmology. A parameter the data pins down tightly is one where changing it would badly inflate the code length; a parameter the data barely constrains is one the optimal code hardly notices. Information is curvature of compressibility.

This is also why score compression (generalized MOPED, §4 [6]) works: the optimal compressed summary is the score itself, — the gradient of the code length at the fiducial model. For weak lensing, a flow or simulator that gives hands you the score by automatic differentiation, and its covariance is the Fisher matrix of the full field — the most information any summary of that map could carry.

10Honest caveats

Compression is throwing information away on purpose — so measure what you are throwing, in the currency that matters: Fisher information.

The caveats below are not vague cautions; each one can be stated as a loss of Fisher information, and for cosmology that is the only currency that counts, because it sets the error bars through the Cramér–Rao bound , i.e. .

1. How much do you lose? The Fisher data-processing inequality

Any compression can only lose information, never create it:

The gap is exactly the information the compression threw away, and it widens the error bars by the Cramér–Rao bound. This is the rigorous version of the demo: PCA's reconstruction looked fine, but as a summary for inference its had collapsed, because it discarded the non-Gaussian modes. The right objective for a scientific compressor is not low RMSE but small .

Worked example (cosmology): why the power spectrum is a lossy compression

For a Gaussian field the two-point function is a sufficient statistic, and the Fisher information on a parameter from the measured power spectrum is the mode-counting formula

where is the sky fraction and the noise — information literally counted mode by mode. For a weak-lensing field this is not the whole story: the convergence is non-Gaussian, so the power spectrum is a lossy summary and . The missing Fisher information is precisely what the bispectrum, peak counts, convergence-map morphology and the field-level methods of §8 recover — and what a linear compressor like PCA destroys. The whole case for higher-order statistics in Euclid and LSST is a statement about this Fisher gap.

2. MOPED's fine print

MOPED/score compression preserves Fisher information exactly only when three things hold: the likelihood is Gaussian, the fiducial model used for the derivatives is close to the truth, and the covariance is known. Weak lensing breaks all three to some degree — the shear likelihood is non-Gaussian, the data covariance is itself uncertain and parameter-dependent, and it must be estimated from a finite set of simulations. Away from the Gaussian/fiducial regime the compressed summary is no longer sufficient, so it can lose information (and, if the fiducial is far off, bias the inference). The fix is to check the compressed posterior against the full one on simulations, not to trust the theorem blindly.

3. Learned compressors inherit their training distribution

A network's code is only valid where its training data lived. If the real universe has a different cosmology, baryonic-feedback model or systematics than the training simulations, the learned "sufficient statistic" is sufficient for the wrong model, and the extra bits it cannot explain show up as the compression gap — which becomes a biased or overconfident posterior. Concretely: a CNN summary of weak lensing trained on one feedback model can shift the recovered when applied to data with different baryon physics. Compressing for information you do not actually have is how a tight, wrong answer is produced. Robustness demands training across the full range of cosmologies and systematics, or marginalising over them.

4. Fidelity is the wrong objective; artifacts are correlated

Optimising a compressor for reconstruction error (an distortion) optimises for the wrong thing: as the demo showed, a code can have excellent RMSE and a collapsed . Worse, lossy-compression errors are not white noise — quantisation and reconstruction residuals are spatially correlated and can mimic signal exactly where it matters (peak counts are most biased precisely at the bright peaks a codec rounds hardest). Any such error must be propagated into the covariance and the final parameter posterior, never assumed negligible.

5. Validate end-to-end, and never reuse simulations

A compressed-likelihood posterior is only trustworthy if its uncertainties are calibrated: check coverage with simulation-based calibration (do the 68% intervals contain the truth 68% of the time?). And building the compressor and running the inference on the same simulations double-counts them and gives falsely tight constraints — the compressor must be trained on held-out runs. Compression and inference are the same activity (§9), which is exactly why the errors of one propagate straight into the other.

Conclusion — the main points, in plain English

If you remember nothing else from this note, remember these.

•  Learning is compression. A good model is a short description of the data. "Fit a model", "find a summary", and "compress" are the same job (Shannon, MDL, Bayes).

•  Classical compression comes in two kinds: lossless (entropy / arithmetic coding, driven by a good predictor) and lossy (transform coding — move to a basis where the data is sparse, keep the big coefficients; wavelets are the cosmologist's version).

•  PCA is the best linear compressor; in cosmology, MOPED takes the radical step of compressing for information (one number per parameter, preserving the Fisher information) rather than for how the map looks.

•  Neural compressors generalise this: an autoencoder is nonlinear PCA; a VAE adds a probabilistic bottleneck and so can also generate; a normalizing flow is exact and invertible, so it reconstructs perfectly and gives an exact likelihood.

•  Fidelity is not information. The demo's lesson: a compressor can have a small reconstruction error yet silently destroy the non-Gaussian structure the science lives on. Compress for the information you came for, not for pixel accuracy.

•  Reconstruction vs realization. A deterministic model hands back the same field, degraded (phases kept, small scales lost); a generative model you sample hands back a new field with the same statistics (phases redrawn).

•  Code length, the score, and the Fisher matrix are one picture: information is the curvature of compressibility — how sharply the number of bits responds to the parameters.

•  Latent variables are the hidden code that generates the data; inference recovers them; a VAE amortizes inference by learning one encoder that answers any datum in a single step.

•  It is all weak lensing. Mass mapping, MOPED, the power spectrum vs the bispectrum, field-level inference, emulators and phase statistics are every one of them a choice of what to compress and what to keep.

•  Be honest about the loss. Lossy compression can only lose Fisher information; validate a compression on the parameter constraints you care about, watch for domain shift, and check that the error bars are calibrated.

11Terminology

Every term used above, in one place.
Entropy
the average number of bits needed to describe data from a distribution — the hard floor for lossless compression.
Lossless / lossy
lossless rebuilds the data exactly (ZIP, PNG); lossy keeps an approximation (JPEG) in exchange for a much smaller size.
Entropy / arithmetic coding
lossless coders that spend bits in proportion to how surprising each symbol is; optimal when driven by an accurate predictive model.
Transform coding
compress by moving to a basis where the data is sparse (few big coefficients), then keeping only those. DCT (JPEG), wavelets (JPEG 2000).
Sparsity
most coefficients being near zero in some basis — the property that makes lossy compression possible.
MDL
Minimum Description Length: pick the model that minimises (model bits) + (data-given-model bits). Occam's razor, quantified.
PCA / KL transform
the optimal linear compression: project onto the top variance directions (covariance eigenvectors).
MOPED
massive optimal data compression for cosmology: compress to one number per parameter while preserving the Fisher information.
Autoencoder
a neural network that compresses then reconstructs through a bottleneck — nonlinear PCA.
VAE
a probabilistic autoencoder with a distribution in the bottleneck; compresses and generates.
Rate–distortion
the theoretical trade-off between code size (rate) and reconstruction error (distortion).
Information bottleneck
learning as compressing the input while keeping the information relevant to a target.
Shannon vs Fisher information
bits needed to describe data (Shannon) vs how sharply data constrain a parameter (Fisher).
Score
the gradient of the log-likelihood (equivalently minus the gradient of the code length) with respect to the parameters; the optimal compressed summary in score compression.
Fisher matrix
the covariance of the score / curvature of the expected code length; sets the best attainable error bars via Cramér–Rao, .
Sufficient statistic
a compression that loses no Fisher information () — the ideal a summary aims for.
Emulator
a trained generative/surrogate model that reproduces expensive simulations on demand — a compression of a whole simulation suite into network weights.
Summary statistic
a lossy compression of a dataset into a few informative numbers (power spectrum, peak counts, bispectrum, a learned code).
Kolmogorov complexity
the length of the shortest program that outputs the data — the ultimate, uncomputable compressor.
Convergence / weak lensing
the projected matter map inferred from the small lensing distortions of galaxy shapes — the field compressed in the demo.
Non-Gaussianity / skewness
departure of a field from Gaussian statistics (here, a skewed one-point PDF from bright peaks) — the information linear compression destroys.

Reproducibility. The demo simulates non-Gaussian (log-normal) weak-lensing convergence maps, then compresses them with PCA (SVD of the training set), undecimated-wavelet top- thresholding, and a convolutional autoencoder trained from scratch (PyTorch), measuring both reconstruction RMSE and recovered skewness versus compression ratio. Every figure and number comes from that single script.
